MAPThree myeloid neoplasms on one axis: the blast count

LO 1What is myelodysplastic syndrome?

Q1. How is MDS defined?
  • Heterogeneous clonal stem cell disorders with maturation defects → disorderly and ineffective hematopoiesis
  • Quantitative and qualitative defects in one, two or all three lines (RBC, neutrophils, platelets)
  • Doesn't meet criteria for acute leukemia, but causes similar problems (marrow suppression) and carries a risk of transformation to AML
  • Primary: idiopathic, slow onset, older (>50). Therapy-related (t-MDS): 2–8 years after genotoxic therapy; progresses to AML more often and faster
Analogy — the sloppy factory

MPN = accelerator stuck, too many good products. MDS = sloppy assembly line: busy factory (hypercellular marrow) but most products are defective and get scrapped before shipping (cytopenias). AML = the line stops; half-built parts pile up.

Q2. What is clonal hematopoiesis, and why does it matter?
  • A clone with ≥1 acquired pathogenic mutation in a cancer gene, in a person with normal blood counts
  • ≈10% of people by age 70; genes TET2, DNMT3A (tumor suppressors regulating DNA methylation)
  • Consequences: 1%/year risk of a hematopoietic neoplasm; pro-inflammatory (worse atherosclerosis, NAFLD, COPD); ↑ RDW (independent mortality predictor)
Q3. What is the MDS classification based on?

Like the leukemias, it combines clinical features, blood and marrow findings, and cytogenetics. You don't need to memorize the WHO 2022 list:

Defined by genetics

  • Low blasts + isolated 5q deletion
  • Low blasts + SF3B1 mutation
  • Biallelic TP53 inactivation

Defined by morphology

  • Low blasts
  • Hypoplastic
  • Increased blasts
  • Any of the above with fibrosis
Step 1

5q− syndrome: older woman, macrocytic anemia, normal or ↑ platelets; responds to lenalidomide. SF3B1 → ringed sideroblasts.

LO 2Cytopenias: symptoms and labs

Q1. How does each cytopenia show up?
Low lineSymptomLab
NeutrophilsInfection↓ ANC; hypogranular, hypolobated neutrophils
Red cellsFatigue, weakness↓ Hb, often macrocytic; most common presenting abnormality
PlateletsBleeding↓ platelet count
  • MDS: mean age ≈70 (range 60–75), men > women; often found on a routine CBC
  • Smear: cells too big, hypogranular, irregular nuclei. Marrow: hypercellular but dysplastic
  • Think MDS in an older patient with unexplained anemia or abnormal counts

MDS smear

  • Hypolobated (pseudo-Pelger-Huët), hypogranular neutrophils

Dysplastic precursors

  • Abnormal nuclei and maturation

MDS aspirate

  • Busy marrow, ugly cells
In-house exam

74-year-old, fatigue, macrocytic pancytopenia, normal B12, hypogranular neutrophils, ringed sideroblasts, blasts <20% → MDS.

Trap

Macrocytic anemia + odd cells mimics B12/folate deficiency ("megaloblastoid" change). Check B12, folate and copper before calling MDS.

Memory tool

Cytopenia triad: "I F B": Infection (WBC), Fatigue (RBC), Bleeding (platelets).

LO 3MDS genetics and complications

Q1. What drives MDS genetically?
  • An initial event damages DNA; secondary "hits" drive progression
  • Driver mutations partly overlap with AML: epigenetic regulators, RNA-splicing factors (SF3B1), transcription factors, TP53
  • Often complex cytogenetic profiles: −7, del(5q), TP53 (−7, complex, TP53 = bad; isolated del(5q) = better)
Q2. How does MDS end?
  • Gradual, progressive; survival from weeks to years
  • Transformation to AML: 30% (slides) / 10–40% (handout)
  • Death from complications of cytopenias: infection, bleeding
  • Treatment: supportive in the elderly; marrow transplant in children and young adults
High yield

Therapy-related MDS (2–8 years after alkylators/radiation; ringed sideroblasts, 5q deletions) progresses faster and more often to AML than primary MDS.

LO 4MDS vs myeloproliferative neoplasms

Q1. How do MPN and MDS differ?
MPNMDSAML
Marrow cellularityIncreasedIncreased (usually)Increased
Marrow blastsNormal↑ but <20%>20%
HematopoiesisEffectiveIneffectiveArrested
Blood countsIncreasedDecreased (cytopenias)↓ normal cells ± ↑ blasts
OrganomegalyCommonUncommonVariable
In-house exam

Same busy marrow, opposite blood: MPN marrow ships product (↑ counts); MDS marrow scraps it (↓ counts).

LO 5Leukemia vs lymphoma; acute vs chronic

Q1. What separates leukemia from lymphoma?

Leukemia

  • Mainly involves bone marrow with circulating tumor cells
  • Myeloid or lymphoid; acute or chronic

Lymphoma

  • Lymphocyte clone forming tissue masses in lymph nodes or extranodal sites
  • CML is a myeloproliferative disorder; CLL is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm, the same disease as small lymphocytic lymphoma (nodes + marrow + blood)

The 2 × 2

  • AML, CML, ALL, CLL
In-house exam

Acute leukemia diagnosis: >20% blasts in the bone marrow.

LO 6AML vs ALL

Q1. How do AML and ALL compare?
AMLALL
WhoAdults, peak >60 (also infants)Children 2–10 (B); adolescents (T)
Risk syndromesTrisomy 21, Bloom, Fanconi anemia, neurofibromatosis; radiation, chemo, benzene, smokingDown syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia
Distinct featuresDIC (APL), gingival hyperplasia (monocytic)Bone/joint pain; CNS, testes, thymus spread
MarkersCD13, CD33 (myeloid); MPO, Auer rodsTdT; B: CD10, CD19, CD20 · T: CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7 (± CD4/CD8)
Good cytogeneticst(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17)Hyperdiploidy >50, t(12;21)
Bad cytogenetics−5/−7, del(7q), t(11q23), TP53, complexHypodiploidy, t(9;22), t(1;19), 14q11 (T)

Age tells the lineage

  • Kids → ALL; adults → AML
Trap

Myeloblasts and lymphoblasts can look alike; flow cytometry markers decide. Auer rods and MPO = myeloid; TdT = lymphoblast.

LO 7Acute vs chronic presentation

Q1. Why does acute leukemia present so differently from chronic?
AcuteChronic
CellsImmature blastsMature and maturing cells
MechanismMaturation arrestIncreased proliferation
ClinicalEarly marrow failure: bleeding, infection, fatigueNon-specific; organ infiltration; marked leukocytosis; late marrow failure
TreatmentUrgentNon-urgent

Bleeding

  • Petechiae, purpura (↓ platelets, DIC)

Gingival hyperplasia

  • Monocytic AML infiltrating gums
Memory tool

Acute = Arrest (blasts pile up, marrow fails now). Chronic = Crowd (mature cells overproduced, fails later).

LO 8AML classification and biology

Q1. What goes wrong in AML?
  • Acquired oncogenic mutations → abnormal myeloid or undifferentiated clone replaces normal marrow → marrow failure
  • Mechanisms: maturation arrest, block in terminal differentiation, ↓ apoptosis
Mutation classExamplesEffect
Transcription factorst(8;21), inv(16) → RUNX1/CBFB fusion; t(15;17) PML-RARαBlock myeloid maturation
Signaling proteinsTyrosine kinasesAlways-on growth/survival
EpigenomeDNA-methylation and chromatin regulatorsAbnormal gene expression
TP53TP53 or its regulatorsComplex karyotype, poor prognosis

WHO classification groups AML by defining genetic abnormalities first (each with its own biology and prognosis), then by differentiation (minimally differentiated, with/without maturation, myelomonocytic, monocytic, erythroid, megakaryocytic).

AML with genetic aberrations

  • Prognosis follows the genetics
Analogy — two hits

AML usually needs a brake failure (transcription factor fusion that blocks maturation) plus a stuck accelerator (signaling mutation that drives growth).

Step 1

M7 (acute megakaryoblastic) is the AML of Down syndrome under age 5. Monocytic AML infiltrates gums and skin.

Q2. How is AML diagnosed?
  • Presentation: peak >60; fatigue, fever, infection, petechial bleeding; pronounced bleeding (DIC) in APL; gingival hyperplasia in monocytic AML
  • Blood: high WBC with circulating blasts, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia
  • Marrow: hypercellular, >20% blasts, normal elements reduced
  • Immunophenotype: CD13, CD33

Myeloblast

  • Fine chromatin, nucleoli, irregular contour

AML smear

  • Sheets of blasts

AML marrow

  • Packed; normal elements gone

Normal marrow

  • Fat + mixed lineages
In-house exam

Vignette labs: WBC 52k, platelets 10k, Hb 7, blasts on smear, marrow 60% blasts, CD13/CD33, inv(16). Prognosis depends on age, counts, molecular findings, speed to remission.

LO 9De novo AML vs AML from MDS

Q1. Why does it matter where AML came from?
De novo AMLMDS-related / therapy-related AML
PatientYoungerOlder, or post-chemotherapy
HistoryAbruptMonths–years of cytopenias
GeneticsBalanced translocations (t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17))Deletions (−5, −7, del(7q)), TP53, complex karyotypes
PrognosisBetterWorse
Memory tool

"Balanced swap in a young patient = good; lost chromosomes in an old marrow = bad."

LO 10AML translocations and prognosis

Q1. Which AML genetics are favorable and which are not?
AbnormalityFusionSubtypePrognosis
t(8;21)RUNX1-RUNX1T1AML with maturation (M2); Auer rodsFavorable
inv(16)CBFB-MYH11Myelomonocytic with abnormal eosinophilsFavorable
t(15;17)PML-RARαAcute promyelocytic leukemia (M3)Very favorable (ATRA)
t(11q23)KMT2A rearrangedMonocytic featuresPoor
−5 / −7, del(7q)—MDS-relatedPoor
TP53, complex—Older, therapy-relatedPoor
In-house exam

Favorable: inv(16), t(8;21), t(15;17). Unfavorable: −7 or −5, del(7q), t(11q23).

Q2. Why is acute promyelocytic leukemia special?
  • t(15;17): PML (15q22) + retinoic acid receptor-α (17) → abnormal RAR blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte
  • Distinct morphology (promyelocytes stuffed with granules and Auer rods, "faggot cells"), DIC, unique prognosis
  • Treatment: all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), a vitamin A derivative, makes the blasts differentiate

APL promyelocyte

  • Bilobed nucleus, heavy granules

Faggot cells

  • Bundles of Auer rods
Memory tool

"15;17 breaks the retinoic acid receptor → vitamin A (ATRA) fixes it."

Step 1

APL: ATRA + arsenic trioxide; watch for differentiation syndrome. Starting chemo in any acute leukemia → tumor lysis syndrome (↑ K⁺, ↑ phosphate, ↑ uric acid, ↓ Ca²⁺) → hydrate + allopurinol/rasburicase.

LO 11How ALL is classified

Q1. What is ALL, and what classifies it?
  • Clonal proliferation of lymphoblasts, immature precursors of B or T cells, from marrow or thymus progenitors
  • Classification: lineage (B vs T by immunophenotype) + recurrent genetic abnormalities (WHO/ICC lists B-ALL by translocation, ploidy, BCR-ABL1-like, etc.)
  • Genetics: transcription factors for B/T development (NOTCH1 for T; PAX5, E2A for B) + growth/survival genes
  • ≈90% have numerical or structural chromosome changes; most common is hyperdiploidy (>50)

B and T maturation

  • TdT in early precursors; markers define lineage

LO 12The patient with ALL

Q1. What does a child with ALL look like?
  • Children 2–10 (B-ALL most common)
  • Marrow failure (lethargy, bleeding, infection) + bone or joint pain
  • Extramedullary spread: CNS (meninges), testes, thymus (T)
  • Blood: high WBC with lymphoblasts, thrombocytopenia, anemia. Marrow: hypercellular blasts, no normal hematopoiesis
  • Relapse: CNS and testes most common; morphology and immunophenotype usually preserved; cytogenetics evolve

ALL blood and marrow

  • Lymphoblasts replace normal cells

Lymphoblasts

  • Scant cytoplasm, fine chromatin

ALL marrow

  • Hypercellular, blasts only
In-house exam

Vignette: WBC 22k, platelets 14k, Hb 8.2, blasts on smear, marrow 80% blasts, CD19, TdT, hyperdiploidy → B-ALL (favorable).

Q2. How does T-ALL differ?
  • Adolescents (often male) with a mediastinal (thymic) mass → difficulty breathing, stridor, hoarseness
  • T-cell markers; higher white counts

Mediastinal mass

  • Stridor, dyspnea, SVC syndrome

T-lymphoblasts

  • Diffuse sheets of blasts
Memory tool

T-ALL = Thymus + Teen + Tight airway; NOTCH1.

Memory tool

"12;21 is good for kids" (12 + 21 = a good age range). "More chromosomes, more cure": hyperdiploid good, hypodiploid bad.

Step 1

Children with ALL: ≈90% cure. Other bad signs: age <1 or >10, WBC >50–100k, T-cell phenotype, CNS disease at diagnosis; t(4;11) KMT2A in infants. Ph+ ALL gets a TKI. LP in every patient.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 74-year-old man has fatigue and macrocytic pancytopenia. B12 and folate are normal. Smear: hypogranular, bilobed neutrophils. Marrow: hypercellular, dysplastic, 8% blasts. Diagnosis?

Ineffective hematopoiesis, dysplasia, blasts <20% → MDS.

2Seven years after chemotherapy for breast cancer, a woman develops cytopenias, dysplasia and a del(5q). Compared with primary MDS, her disease will most likely:

Therapy-related MDS (2–8 years after genotoxic therapy) does worse.

3Which feature best separates an MPN from MDS?

Both marrows are busy; MPN is effective (↑ counts), MDS ineffective (cytopenias).

4What marrow blast percentage defines acute leukemia in this course?

>20% blasts.

5A 65-year-old has fatigue, fever, petechiae and swollen gums. WBC 52k with blasts that are CD13+ and CD33+. Diagnosis?

CD13/CD33 = myeloid; gingival hyperplasia = monocytic AML.

6A 38-year-old has DIC and purpura. Marrow is packed with promyelocytes containing bundles of Auer rods. Which therapy targets the molecular defect?

APL, t(15;17) PML-RARα → ATRA (± arsenic).

7Which AML cytogenetic finding carries a poor prognosis?

−5/−7, del(7q), t(11q23), TP53, complex = unfavorable.

8Compared with de novo AML, AML arising from MDS typically has:

MDS- and therapy-related AML do worse.

9A 4-year-old has fever, petechiae and bone pain. Marrow: 80% blasts that are TdT+, CD10+, CD19+. Most likely diagnosis?

TdT = lymphoblast; CD10/CD19 = B.

10A 16-year-old boy has stridor and a mediastinal mass; WBC is very high with TdT+ CD3+ CD7+ blasts. Which gene is classically involved?

T-ALL: thymic mass in teens; NOTCH1.

11Which B-ALL finding predicts the best outcome?

Hyperdiploidy and t(12;21) are favorable.

12A boy treated for ALL relapses 2 years later. Besides the marrow, which site is most common?

Sanctuary sites: CNS and testes.

13Which syndrome raises the risk of both AML and ALL?

Trisomy 21 appears on both lists (AML: + Bloom, Fanconi, NF; ALL: + ataxia-telangiectasia).
